name: Aldabra Atoll
subtitle: A natural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1982.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The atoll is comprised of four large coral islands which enclose a shallow lagoon; the group of islands is itself surrounded by a coral reef. Due to difficulties of access and the atoll's isolation, Aldabra has been protected from human influence and thus retains some 152,000 giant tortoises, the world's largest population of this reptile.”
Wikipedia calls Aldabra the world's second-largest coral atoll, after Kiritimati. It belongs to the Outer Islands of the Seychelles, 1,120 km south-west of the capital Victoria on Mahé.
The name comes from Arab seafarers, who named the atoll for its harsh, sun-baked environment, and Portuguese navigators visited in 1511.

In the middle of the 18th century it became a dependency of the French colony of Réunion, and expeditions came to capture the Aldabra giant tortoises. There is no surface fresh water, so explorers exploited tortoises, turtles and fish rather than settling.

National Geographic described Aldabra in 2019 as one of the world's largest coral atolls, more than 700 miles west of Mahé, with around 100,000 giant tortoises. Tortoises once lived on most islands of the Indian Ocean until 17th-century sailors hunted them for provisions, because they can survive months without water or food.

Aldabra was the only island in the ocean basin where a few thousand survived. It was set aside as a special reserve in the 1980s and is a natural World Heritage site, managed by the Seychelles Island Foundation.

The article calls the atoll extremely inhospitable: razor-sharp coral rock, no fresh water, many mosquitoes and heat. Other wildlife includes flightless Aldabra rails, coconut crabs the size of dinner plates, frigatebirds and sharks.
